title: Lipid Chemistry
objectives: Understand the structure and classification of lipids
Describe the chemical properties and biological roles of fatty acids, triglycerides, phospholipids, and steroids
Explain the significance of lipids in energy storage, membrane structure, and signaling
Analyze the metabolic pathways involving lipids, including β-oxidation and lipid biosynthesis

overview.title: Lipid Overview
overview.content:
Lipids are a diverse group of hydrophobic or amphipathic molecules that include fats, oils, phospholipids, steroids, and waxes. They are insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents. Lipids play critical roles in energy storage, cell membrane structure, and signaling. The main classes of lipids include fatty acids, glycerolipids (e.g., triglycerides), phospholipids, sphingolipids, and sterols (e.g., cholesterol).

Biological Significance

  • Energy Storage: Triglycerides store more energy per gram than carbohydrates or proteins.
  • Membrane Structure: Phospholipids and cholesterol form the lipid bilayer of cell membranes.
  • Signaling: Steroid hormones (e.g., testosterone, estrogen) and eicosanoids (e.g., prostaglandins) regulate physiological processes.
  • Insulation and Protection: Fats insulate the body and cushion organs.

Key Lipid Classes

Simple Lipids

  • Fatty acids (saturated, unsaturated)
  • Triglycerides (triacylglycerols)
  • Waxes

Complex Lipids

  • Phospholipids (e.g., phosphatidylcholine)
  • Sphingolipids (e.g., sphingomyelin)
  • Glycolipids (e.g., cerebrosides)

Derived Lipids

  • Steroids (e.g., cholesterol, hormones)
  • Eicosanoids (e.g., prostaglandins)
  • Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K)

key_concepts.title: Key Concepts
key_concepts.content:
Fatty Acid Structure

Definition: Carboxylic acids with long hydrocarbon chains (4-36 carbons).

Types: Saturated (no double bonds), unsaturated (one or more double bonds), essential (must be obtained from diet).

Phospholipid Bilayer

Definition: Amphipathic molecules with hydrophilic heads (phosphate group) and hydrophobic tails (fatty acids).

Function: Forms the basic structure of cell membranes, creating a selective barrier.

Cholesterol

Role: Modulates membrane fluidity and serves as a precursor for steroid hormones and bile acids.

Transport: Carried in blood by lipoproteins (LDL, HDL).

chemical_reactions.title: Chemical Reactions
chemical_reactions.content:
Hydrolysis and Esterification

Hydrolysis: Triglycerides are broken down into glycerol and fatty acids (e.g., by lipases).

Esterification: Glycerol reacts with fatty acids to form triglycerides (e.g., fat storage).

Saponification

Process: Alkaline hydrolysis of triglycerides produces soap (fatty acid salts) and glycerol.

Peroxidation

Process: Oxidative degradation of unsaturated lipids, producing free radicals.

Significance: Contributes to cell damage and aging; prevented by antioxidants (e.g., vitamin E).

biological_roles.title: Biological Roles
biological_roles.content:
Energy Storage and Metabolism

β-Oxidation: Fatty acids are broken down in mitochondria to produce acetyl-CoA for the TCA cycle.

Ketogenesis: Acetyl-CoA is converted into ketone bodies during fasting or starvation.

Membrane Structure

Fluidity: Unsaturated fatty acids and cholesterol maintain membrane flexibility.

Lipid Rafts: Microdomains enriched in cholesterol and sphingolipids, involved in signaling.

Signaling

Steroid Hormones: Derived from cholesterol (e.g., cortisol, estrogen).

Eicosanoids: Signaling molecules derived from arachidonic acid (e.g., prostaglandins, leukotrienes).

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
What is the difference between LDL and HDL?+
LDL ('bad' cholesterol) delivers cholesterol to tissues; HDL ('good' cholesterol) removes excess cholesterol for excretion.
Why are trans fats harmful?+
Trans fats increase LDL, decrease HDL, and promote inflammation, raising cardiovascular disease risk.
How do lipids contribute to obesity?+
Excess calories are stored as triglycerides in adipose tissue, leading to obesity when intake exceeds energy expenditure.
What is the role of bile acids in lipid digestion?+
Bile acids emulsify dietary fats, increasing surface area for lipase action in the small intestine.
